newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Boeing defends McDonnell merger, rivals unmoved.
newsitem.headline: Boeing defends McDonnell merger, rivals unmoved.

text.p: Boeing Co pursued its efforts on Friday to convince the European Commission and rival aviation companies to allow its $14 billion merger with McDonnell Douglas Corp, but sources said it met with little sympathy.
While the participants at the second day of a two-day closed-door hearing remained strictly tight-lipped, sources familiar with the EU's merger investigation noted positions had hardly changed.
"They have not convinced us anyway," an EU source said.

The Commission's hearing, which gathered about 20 Boeing executives and many representatives from Airbus Industrie and its partners, was not meant to reach conclusions, but to allow all parties to air their views about the takeover as required in the EU's merger control law.
Having respected the procedure, the Commission's services will now prepare a draft decision for a meeting of national competition experts from the bloc's 15 states on July 4.

The experts will be free that day from stock market pressure -- it being Independence Day holiday in the United States -- but may feel the burden of an early decision by the U.S. Federal Trade Commission if all goes according to schedule.
The FTC has until July 1 to make its decision after Boeing and McDonnell Douglas certified they had filed the documents required. The EU Commission itself must reach a final verdict by July 31.
Although nobody would prejudge the EU's decision at this early stage, there is a clear feeling that the Commission will not backtrack on its strong objections to the deal.
Nor is European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert likely to swallow his harsh comments about Boeing's long-term supply contracts with big American airlines.

The ball is increasingly in Boeing's court. But the U.S. giant will probably not make any significant concession until it sees whether the FTC, which has been keeping its cards close to its chest, shares any of the EU's competition concerns, industry and EU sources said.
Boeing and others have operated on the assumption that the Americans are likely to be more favourable to the merger than the EU.

In a statement to Boeing in May, the Commission argued in detail that Boeing, which already controls 64 percent of the world's market for large commercial aircraft, would see its position strengthened through McDonnell's still significant customer base and the use of military subsidies.
McDonnell Douglas derives about 70 percent of its total business from the defence and space sector.

Airbus partners British Aerospace (BAe) and Daimler-Benz Aerospace (DASA) have called for a re-negotiation of a 1992 EU-U.S. agreement over aircraft subsidies claiming that the industry gets far more public support on the other side of the Atlantic.

BAe and DASA calls, in the meantime, to turn Airbus into an independent company capable of rivalling Boeing are meeting with resistance at Aerospatiale, the consortium's other key shareholder, and its parent French government.

Leaving the civil aviation market at the mercy of Boeing and Airbus -- which has about 30 percent of the world's market -- is unlikely to satisfy the Commission, which fears this might turn into a 'cosy duopoly'.

If the Commission feels that Airbus will not overcome soon its problems in converting to a 'single corporate entity' and launching its A3XX wide-bodied aircraft to rival Boeing's jumbo jet monopoly, it is even less likely to agree a deal which would make Boeing even stronger.

The merger was defended on the first day of the hearing on Thursday by Boeing's executive vice president of the commercial airplane group, Dick Albrecht, and the head of the merger transition team, Jerry King.
On Friday it was the turn of Airbus's managing director, Jean Pierson, to provide evidence on the implications of the merger.
Airbus's individual partners were also due to comment on aspects not covered by Airbus. But U.S. military aircraft maker Lockheed Martin was not represented contrary to expectations.
